speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on this motion. I concur with the main intent of it, but we have to rethink what has been done. One can assume that the motion has at least in part been precipitated by the so-called leaked document which seems to indicate that we are not seeing a new vision and a change in the way things will be done. Despite the rather glowing report card which the Parliamentary Secretary gave, we have to consider why this matter generates so much discussion. If things have advanced as quickly as the Parliamentary Secretary has indicated to us they have, if things are as good as he has indicated to us they are, then why is it that none of us really has the time to explore the issues in the depth that we know need to be explored? There are so many problems and so many complications.
One thing about the document as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), said, there does not seem to be a thrust for substantive change in policy
but rather a sort of cosmetic better communications policy. In one section it says that the old ways have not worked. We know that. In another section it says that we are not seeking dramatic change. Why not, Mr. Speaker? The time is now for dramatic change if we have the political will to change the way we have treated aboriginal people in this country. I do not think we have yet seen a government that has the political will.
With all due respect to my colleague from Cochrane, whom I respect very much for the work he has done on aboriginal issues, his Liberal Government created much of this legacy. The 1969 White Paper of Jean Chretien proposed that the vision would be for assimilation. These are not new problems. I suppose in that sense I can be somewhat sympathetic to the current Government that it is having to deal with a situation which has gone on for a very long time and which neither the previous Government nor this one have taken in hand to address appropriately. It is sort of like the acid rain question. Lots of consultation. Let us consult some more. At the same time the problem keeps eroding our country. It keeps eating away at the respect that we have for one another, for the honour we have for all of our citizens.
I notice that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) today spoke about nuclear submarines and why we need submarines for our sovereignty. I beg to differ. Our sovereignty will not be defined by hardware in such things as nuclear submarines. It will be defined by our strength as a people. Nowhere in Canada does the way that we have dealt with aboriginal issues and rights exemplify our weakness as a people. If we look at other examples of sovereignty, we see in Vietnam that there was a lot of hardware and many troops but it was the will of the people who established sovereignty and won the war.
I want to give an example which I think exemplifies what we are really talking about. There are a lot of statistics, and they have been talked about today, but we are really talking about fairness and justice and correcting historical wrongs. One of my constituents is a man named Elijah Smith, a respected elder in the Yukon. He fought in World War II for his country, Canada. He returned home to the Yukon to establish the first native organization there because he realized that only by working together would any advancement be made. The native people could not wait for the rest of Canada to give it to them.
Fortunately, Mr. Smith did not have to give up his life for his country, but he did have to give up his Indian status, his definition as a person, in order to fight for this country. When the war was over he did not receive the same benefits, such as land, as many non-native members of the Armed Forces. When he returned from the battles he still did not have the right to vote in the country for which he had just fought. That is really what this is all about.
Today Elijah Smith and many like him still fight for their children and grandchildren, the Indian people. He is in the
May 11, 1988

forefront of such issues as land claims. Having fought in World War II for Canada, we really have to ask why Elijah Smith has to fight today for the rights of his people.
I suggest that if previous Governments and the current Government had the political will, we would not be seeing yet another document that talks about consultation. We would be seeing a document that talks about implementation, about what we are really going to do. Nowhere is this better exemplified than in the question of land claims and the issue of aboriginal title.
As most people will know, the aboriginal people were not conquered. There were a number of treaties signed, but there were a number of areas where they were not signed, and that is the basis of the land claims negotiations. They were not a conquered people and therefore some compensation for lands assumed must be made. However, land claims is not just about land, it is also about how Canada's first people can regain the culture they have had taken away and destroyed. Let me give an example of that.
If you are a parent and your child is six years old and you are told it must go away, sometimes many miles away, to a strange place where they do not speak your language, where brothers and sisters will be separated and not allowed to talk to each other, you would be quite surprised. When you expressed some objection you would be told that you are doing something good for your child, something that will ensure your child's future, and that you have no choice. If you are the child and you are put on a bus and you said goodbye to your parents and went to a strange place where you are not allowed to speak your language and are told that two months of the year you will be allowed to go home, then you would see what we are dealing with today. We are dealing first with an attempt to destroy a culture. That did not work so then came an attempt to assimilate. That has not worked so now we are trying to find ways to settle it just a little bit better, but we are still not very serious about it.
This did not happen hundreds of years ago, as most people will know, but 20 years ago. If you wished to fight for your children, or study for a profession, or married a non-native person, you had to give up your Indian status, your definition as a person. Today of course that is quite inconceivable, but I want to mention some areas where this kind of philosophy continues in many of the policies we see today.
While there are other areas of the country where the same issues exist, I want to speak about my own area where I can do so most authoritatively concerning land claims. In the Yukon and the Northwest Territories the majority of the land, some 96 per cent in the Yukon, is controlled by the federal Government. Until land claims are settled no economic development can take place for native people or non-native people in a comprehensive way. It follows that no constitutional development can take place. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) has said until the
Supply
Territories can become economically self-sufficient, province-hood will not be a possibility. We are in a catch-22 situation. I believe very strongly that if there is a will to settle the land claims issue in a fair and just way, it will be done. I will give an example.
There is an excellent process taking place in the Yukon now where the three parties, the Indians, the Yukon Government and the federal Government, are negotiating. They travel from community to community so that people will understand what is taking place. After a lot of difficulty because the process is tough, they will come to a point where all three parties can agree. That agreement is then sent back to Ottawa to the bureaucrats, as my friend from Cochrane-Superior defined them, who know nothing about the experience or the history of this part of the country. They then start to assess and analyse the agreement and very often they assess it and analyse it right out of existence.
We have seen many examples of the negotiating process where there is certainly a non-political role. There is another role that very clearly is political. Clearly in this instance the Minister, in all of the land claims settlements, must say directly to his officials that he wants these land claims to be settled, that he wants the negotiation process to conclude in a fair and just way for everyone concerned. Yet we have this situation of agreements being made and then coming back to Ottawa where they are torn apart. This is not a helpful process. In fact, it is a very destructive process for aboriginal people as well as others.
The Lubicon land claim hardly needs to be repeated in the House. It is a legacy of 50 years where the claim still has not been settled, and there has been a refusal to appoint a mediator requested by the people. Why is there this kind of resistance? This is exactly the basis for the motion we are debating. It is the philosophy and the will to make a dramatic change and yet we have this leaked document which says no, we are not going to make a dramatic change. Dramatic changes are certainly needed. I would like to say a few words about the idea of self-government. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary stated that talks are going on right now about the issue of self-government and further constitutional talks.
Yet the document which the Hon. Member referred to today talks about how the Department has received some 60 proposals representing 228 bands to initiate negotiations on self-government. The response in that document is to talk about the lack of resources to handle the growing number of community requests posing a serious threat to a strategy of demonstrating that practical arrangements can be worked out at the local level without constitutional changes. This is not the first time where the consultation process has been undertaken and the outcome defined in another forum. Therefore, I think we can quite readily understand the concern, indeed the suspicion, of many aboriginal groups and those of us who are not aboriginal people that if these matters are not settled we will all suffer, not just the aboriginal people. The United Nations has already found that we have not honoured some of

May 11, 1988
Supply
our treaties and have shown discrimination. This is a shame to all of us.
I would like to touch on a few topics about which the Minister spoke as showing great improvement. Housing is one area in which he said some interesting improvements had been made. Figures in a report by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation of May, 1987, differ from those presented by the Minister who said that 20 years ago less than half of native housing had electricity. He said that two-thirds of the homes now have electricity available and that one-sixth did not have water supply.
However, according to this report, 36 per cent of on-reserve units are crowded as opposed to 2.3 per cent in the general population. We see that 43 per cent of the housing units are in need of major repairs as opposed to 13 per cent throughout Canada. Forty per cent do not have access to running water, indoor toilets, or bathing facilities, as opposed to 1 per cent across Canada.
Therefore, if we are to accept the Parliamentary Secretary's contention that housing has improved, it has certainly improved darn little. I am not sure that many aboriginal people would be able to accept that glowing report.
There are some rather ill-planned programs which exemplify the lack of a new political will and dramatic action. There has been an attempt, for a number of years now, to have joint funding for housing between the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and Canada Mortgage and Housing. In my area people have received notices in the mail recently that their rents will go up by some 30 per cent to 100 per cent. If this happened in Toronto there would be riots. The people of one community have decided that, with summer coming, they will live in their tents because they cannot afford this housing, this great program which was to solve this problem for Indian people.
In another community three people have had to move out of the housing. The band has to keep up payments for the housing and is trying to rent the housing to a non-member of the band in order that they will not lose it. This is an absolutely ludicrous situation.
With Bill C-31 and the reinstatement of people who lost their status-another bureaucratic decision taken without any reference to the culture or the way in which the community operated-we see an increased need for housing and an increased problem without a direct focus on an answer to this problem.
The whole question of who is an Indian and who is not an Indian relates very much to this motion. The Government, which is willing to spend $7 billion, $8 billion, or $16 billion on nuclear submarines, is not willing to spend the money to address this problem. We therefore try to redefine who is an Indian. Aboriginal people know who the aboriginal people are,
but the bureaucracy and Government decide to fool around with that and decide who is and who is not.
I referred to the loss of status for a variety of reasons. However, even when bands are attempting to constitute their membership, there are so many rules and hurdles about who is an Indian and who is not that it is ridiculous. It is the stuff of a good satire, but it is a tragedy for the bands which are attempting to build their communities and address the kinds of problems outlined in this motion. For example, band members are not allowed to transfer to another band. As the motion indicates, no new band can be created.
In my own constituency a band was amalgamated with another band in the 1950s by an Indian agent who thought that since they were all Indian people he could put them all together and it would not matter. Of course, that was totally ignorant of the culture and the way in which the band functioned. It has not worked, and the Government is not now prepared to separate those bands and redress that wrong.
Language defines a culture. The Tungavik of Nunavut, for example, want very much to have language included as part of their land claim. That may be a strange concept to some people. However, if one understands the culture one will understand the way in which we have attempted to destroy the language of a people that is absolutely key to their development. On that particular issue the Government has said no. However, the Inuit are very clear about the importance of their language, not just because it is all very interesting to have Inuktitut spoken, but because it is an essential part of their life.
As another example, the Secretary of State has said that we will have a national aboriginal language centre. Languages are regional, and it is very difficult for various areas to get funding for language development. The Six Nations Reserve, for example, which has one of the largest language programs in Canada, has been seeking five-year funding to get a really serious language program going. They cannot wait for 5 or 10 years. These languages are disappearing. Surely Canada must preserve the sacred trust of language.
There are many other issues including the need for band administration funding. Cut-backs, rumoured and real, continue and make it very difficult for the self-government and sound administration which we expect of the bands.
I am happy to support this motion on behalf of my Party. Tinkering with a few programs and making changes here and there is not the solution. The solution is a new vision and a political will to make sure, once and for all, that we institute the fairness and justice which aboriginal people deserve.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would my colleague from the Yukon give us a sense of the major priorities which she feels a New Democratic Party Government would wish to put into place with respect to Indian communities after an election?
May 11, 1988

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly the most crucial aspect is to have control over one's life. We see many instances in which people make decisions for other people and decide how they should live by them. Whoever defines the problem defines the solution. For many years non-aboriginal people have talked about "the Indian problem". Aboriginal people, on the other hand, have talked about "the white problem". There is something to be said in the definition of the problem.
The only answer for all people is to have a degree and element of control over their own life and their own decision making, whatever form that should take. That form should be decided jointly by the aboriginal communities, the territorial and provincial Governments, and the federal Government.
The very fact that, as this document says, the Department has received 60 proposals representing 228 bands asking to initiate negotiations on self-government indicates the priority for people, which is just plain common sense. Imagine that, as I said in my speech, people who fought for their country and wanted to become a doctor or marry a non-native had to become enfranchised or say "I am not a native person". That is ludicrous.
The priority for a New Democratic Government or any Government must be to facilitate the self-determination of aboriginal people on appropriate cultural terms, in band administration and development, in economic development, and in constitutional development.
If one does not have some control over one's life, one is left with what this document defines as the old ways. The old ways are our defining for others what they should do to make their life better, generally in a culture that we do not even understand.
A New Democratic Government will change that. Indeed, any Government must change that in order for there to be any justice at all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for her support for the motion, and I commend her for an excellent speech. The Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) will be familiar with the very important claim that is being negotiated in the North, in her constituency. It is the claim being negotiated between the Government of Canada and the Council for Yukon Indians.
The motion makes reference to aboriginal claims. We all know that the much heralded new claims policy fell well short of the recommendations contained in the Coolican report. Nevertheless, it is a new claims policy.
Does she believe this has facilitated to any degree at all the settlement of that claim? Can she tell the House, from her own knowledge, what exactly are the obstacles at the moment? So far only one claim has been settled in the North, with the Inuvialuit who occupy the delta of the Mackenzie River. It is the so-called Committee for Peoples' Entitlement Claim.
Supply
We have long expected a settlement in the Yukon but there seems to be delay upon delay. What are the obstacles that she has been able to detect?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the claims policy to which the Hon. Member refers certainly ran into a lot of deep water. It took two years to develop, which I find incomprehensible, given that the Yukon land claim has gone on for over 15 years. I think the issues were fairly clear.
My colleague referred to the impediment to the land claims settlement. I must reiterate what I said in my speech. There is a fairly open process now, with a lot of consultation with the communities. There is agreement on some major issues and there is still some outstanding disagreement, but of course I am not party to the ongoing negotiations.
The point I want to stress is that the Minister must convey to his Department the message that this land claim must be settled. There is the political will at the local level and there has been agreement on substantive issues. The problem arises when the strings are pulled from Ottawa, where there is no experience with what will work in the Yukon.
It is time we stopped working from the book and began thinking about what is practical, reasonable, and culturally appropriate for native people and non-native people in these land claims. Rather than formulate a bureaucratic, technically perfect document, let us look at what will work. We know well what has not worked, so there is a good basis upon which to settle the claims, if the Minister will make a strong statement to his Department that this must be settled now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member on her speech. What are her views on the whole question of native child welfare? I believe I heard the Parliamentary Secretary suggest that native people are not interested in day care but want to give native child welfare a higher priority.
I believe I heard the Minister's representative suggest that money was going into this function. On the other hand, we have had complaints from aboriginal groups in Alberta and Manitoba that there is no funding going toward support services for families to help them strengthen families, provide their own foster homes, and care for their own children.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the whole issue of child welfare, like the cultural and language issues, is very important. One way to destroy a culture is to make sure the children are estranged from it, so that they lose the language and are detached from the family unit.
Child welfare involves the same issue of control over one's life and destiny.
During my speech I referred to the leaked document and some of its aspects which are rather cosmetic and do not address basic issues. The Parliamentary Secretary will be glad to hear me refer to something that is positive and for which I will hold the Government accountable. It states that child

May 11, 1988
Supply
welfare is already identified as a first priority, and that the Government will be prepared to seek authority to lift the moratorium on new agreements and begin consultations in 1988. I hope that is true because the issue of child welfare is extremely important in aboriginal communities, as I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary is very well aware.
The sad fact is that generations of children were separated from their families and did not grow up in a family unit where they had role models. It has been a tragic legacy for aboriginal people and a shame for this country.
After quoting some aspects of this document which are less hopeful, I believe this is a positive one that I look forward to seeing implemented.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, due to a meeting of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development, I regret that I have not been here to listen to all the debate. I would like to have heard the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) who moved the motion, because as a member of the same committee I certainly know that he has dedicated much of his interest and concern to this subject.
I* heard the beginning of his remarks, which he began appropriately by talking in terms of justice and injustice. Certainly this Parliament must address injustice toward native people generally, not only in this debate but in a constant attempt to find equal opportunity to build upon the full potential of the native people of Canada. When speaking of justice or injustice in terms of dollars, no matter how we argue the percentages we see that this Government has made a particularly important financial contribution.
In fact it is a substantial greater contribution than was made by the previous Government in the four years from 1980 to 1984. I suppose there is a bit of irony that the Member who proposed the motion was part of the Government which did not see justice in terms of dollars because its commitment was a lesser commitment than that of the current Government. Justice, of course, is not found in terms of dollars. If in fact one is a victim of injustice, as so many native people seem to be, any form of natural justice seems painfully slow as native people find their potential in Canada.
If one is part of that 30 per cent of the native population which can be found in the Canadian penitentiary system, if one is part of that penitentiary population, there in part because of cultural differences or because of lost or missed opportunity, one finds that justice is indeed slow. Those living on the streets of Vancouver, Toronto, or Montreal, broken down by drugs, alcohol or prostitution, cut off from their natural friends and relatives, are indeed victims of the system. We must address those very real, human concerns.
Those who are trying to find their way through the maze of Bill C-31 in order to find their status and dignity in that sense
indeed will find that to be a difficult procedure as well. Certainly we can look at it negatively, as the Opposition must, but we must also try to look at the record which shows that the Government has made an increasing commitment of funds and effort to try to bring about change.
It is very easy just to deal with the status quo. Any longterm bureaucracy, establishment, or business unit always resists change. The Government has tried to bring about change and correct injustice with Bill C-31. As a result, over 40,000 Canadians have found their status. Another 40,000 Canadians have gained medical, dental, and educational benefits as well. There is a very positive story with respect to Bill C-31 for those people who now have health benefits and improvements in educational opportunities.
I would like to put some of our programs on record so that we can see the positive side. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development deals with programs and services which cover the entire range of services any modern community has come to expect and demand. In the current year the budget for Indian services, capital, economic development, local government support, education, and welfare totals $2.1 billion. That is $2.1 billion of the funds of Canadian taxpayers. It is a 9.8 per cent increase over the previous year. I would have to say that it is a pretty good increase during a period of financial restraint and attempts to bring the deficit under control.
Those of us who serve on the Standing Committee of Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development and are particularly concerned about the Indian people would want to say that it is not enough. I am sure, when we come down to our report on Bill C-31, we will be advocating more to be done in many areas for the Indian people. I suppose when it does come down to the question of talking in terms of dollars-how much is enough-the answer is always "more".
Over the past 10 years there has been significant and continuing improvement in the ability of Indian Governments to provide the basic amenities and services to their people. I will give a bit of credit to the previous administration, because even it tried to improve the budget. In 1988-89 we are looking at a capital budget that totals $341 million. This is $341 million which will provide roads, sewers, water treatment plants, electrification, community buildings, and housing.
For example, one area about which I hear constant concern from native people is the area of housing. Sometimes one would think that nothing is ever done because we hear the complaints so often. However, in 1988-89, some $118 million will be used to assist Indian communities in meeting the household needs of their communities. It should be understood this is not an outright grant but a subsidy, the level of which depends upon the geographical location of the community. A contribution is made to an Indian band to assist in defraying the costs of construction of a house. Since 1979 there has been a requirement that these houses be built to the standards of the National Building Code. In addition, the band secures
May 11, 1988

additional financing above the subsidy level to complete the unit.
In the last five years, 14,000 new homes and over 17,000 renovations have been completed on Indian reserves. It is never enough, but that is 14,000 new families located in homes in which they can take a sense of pride and where their children can bring friends, homes where enduring family traditions can be built.
Let us look more closely at the situation of housing in Indian communities. The quality of Indian housing has improved and will continue to improve. The overcrowding problem has been reduced considerably. In 1977 there was an average of 5.9 inhabitants per reserve house. Today we are looking at a number below 5.0 inhabitants per house, in spite of an increase in the birth rate. Over the past 10 years there has also been a significant improvement in the number of Indian communities that have access to the normal electrical services most people take for granted. By 1986-87, 87 per cent of on-reserve houses had full electrical service. Today the majority of Indian communities are serviced by provincial electric grids rather than by diesel generated systems. That integration of systems has indeed helped.
However, one would still wonder what kind of a backward nation we are when 1 per cent, 2 per cent, 10 per cent, or 12 per cent of houses are not electrified in Canada today. I find it incredible when I travel internationally and see homes without electricity. Surely electricity is a basic requirement in the Canadian lifestyle.
There is also an important side benefit to the housing program in terms of its impact on the Indian community. Virtually 100 per cent of home construction and renovation is managed by Indian bands themselves using Indian labour and, where possible, Indian supplied materials. This provides needed jobs in the Indian community and helps to reduce dependence on welfare. It also provides an opportunity to develop skills such as those of electricians and carpenters, skills that are essential to the long-term health and vitality of the community.
During the 1980s there has also been a significant improvement in the number and quality of houses constructed on Indian reserves. Adherence to the National Building Code has meant that quality housing is being built that will last well beyond what was once considered the norm in Indian communities. In raw statistical terms, the current budget foresees in this year that some 2,700 houses will be built, and a further 2,300 units will be renovated. This is not every house and does not go anywhere near the demand, but it is not an insignificant contribution by the people of Canada to the native community of Canada to assist in approving the housing situation.
Whenever one visits an Indian community one is undoubtedly aware of how vital and important education is for the future. Healthy communities that are capable of directing their own

destinies require the skills and knowledge of modern education. This modern education system is evolving throughout Canada among native people. The Department currently supports more than 82,000 Indian students enrolled in elementary and secondary schools. Approximately 50 per cent of those students attend provincial schools, 28 per cent are in band operated schools, and the remainder are in federal schools.
Over 14 years ago the federal Government began transferring control of Indian education to bands. I noticed that even today when members of the Mohawk tribe appeared before the committee they stated that one of their major priorities was to gain full control of their own post-secondary and elementary education system. At the present time this process is being accelerated. In the past fiscal year a further 18 schools representing 2,300 students have been transferred. This year it is planned that a further 27 schools will be transferred. By 1991 it is anticipated that most Indian students will attend band or provincial schools. That is a pretty large sociological change over a brief period of time, and a tribute both to the previous Government and this Government that we should be accelerating that pace and measure of control.
The past decade has also seen an impressive school construction program. A significant portion of the capital budget has been allocated to this objective, resulting in a full 143 school facilities being built or renovated over the past 10 years. In 1986-87, there were 243 band operated schools compared with 135 in 1980-81. That is a 100 per cent improvement. The five-year, long-term capital plan foresees expenditures of approximately $290 million, comprising 1,800 school projects.
Perhaps the most dramatic evidence came last September in Manitoba. For years northern Manitoban Indian children have had to leave their communities and travel south, if they wished to carry on their education beyond grade school. It is often a traumatic experience, and we found that very few made it through to graduation. Last fall six new schools were opened in northern Manitoba. For example, the school at Cross Lake was a $16.7 million project, the largest capital project ever undertaken by a band and the Department in an Indian community.
New and modern educational facilities are a necessary part of any education system. However, quality represents a partnership between teachers, students, and the community. That is why the Government believes that local control and parental involvement are so important. Indeed, one can see the impact of those factors on the performance of Indian children in the schools today. More Indian children are staying in school longer, more children are graduating from high school, and more young adults are going on to post-secondary education.
In addition to those statistics, there are many other government programs such as the one 1 attended on Friday in my community. This was a manpower program that I assisted in starting, and here I found 12 native people aged from 19 or 20 to 40. The highest level that had been attained by those people

ordinarily would have been active in that committee were engaged in this debate. However, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West was present, and I believe he listened to the testimony of the Blackfoot tribe of Treaty 7 in the southern part of the Province of Alberta.
He will therefore know that this tribe has a particular problem at the present time with the Government of Canada concerning a cattle claim settlement. A long time ago the treaty allowed for those people to receive a certain number of cattle. That obligation was never met. It is the history of Canada that, in the main, these treaties were ignored. But, in the life of the last administration, finally an agreement was reached. Instead of cattle there was to be a cash compensation. That money was delivered to the tribe and distributed among its members. To their utter amazement when they received their regular social assistance they discovered that the amount of money received by each individual was subtracted from the social assistance payment. This seemed to them to be a violation, and I share this feeling. It was a violation of a treaty obligation. It was taking from one pocket of government and putting it back into the other pocket. It is a Peter and Paul situation.
The Hon. Member heard the grievance expressed this afternoon. He probably is familiar with the problem. Therefore, I wish to ask him whether he proposes to take to the Government the request that this be dealt with in a just fashion. What exact steps does he intend to take or suggest that the committee take regarding the grievance of the Blackfoot tribe on its treaty rights?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has said that our responsibility is to define the potential of the aboriginal people. I should like to suggest that our task is to ensure that the Indian people have the resources to utilize their demonstrated skills, and not some vague "potential" that we are going to define. The Indian people should have control over the establishment of their own needs.
While there are many issues that have been discussed today, I should like to focus on two which relate to the manner of funding Indian bands and the extent of such funding.
The late receipt of funds by Indian bands leads to tremendous administrative problems. Payments are inevitably late, with the result that band staff cannot be paid. Often, the band has to draw upon a bank overdraft, or borrow funds in some other manner in order to discharge its obligations. Because bank charges cannot be included in band budgets, funds for such charges have to come out of yet another budget, thus putting tremendous administrative stresses on the bands.
In addition to addressing the matter of late payments, I would ask the Hon. Member to address the level of band funding in respect of administrative functions. In terms of the programs that have been discussed during the course of this debate, and the implementation thereof, Indian bands are carrying a tremendous load. They cannot afford to pay band staff salaries that are comparable to those available on the open market, with the result that staff is lost to employment that offers higher salaries and greater security.
Band administration is something that is very difficult, and I would be interested in having the Hon. Member's views on that.

The Government has embarked upon a program of education for band administrators. This is something that is done through native education centres and our universities.
In order to bring about greater efficiency, those handling the business transactions of the native communities need to be better educated. Toward that end, new educational programs are being developed, and existing ones expanded. That is something that is happening on a daily basis.
On the matter of the transfer of funds, hopefully that will improve as we move to more self-government, self-administration. The policy of this Government is to move toward selfgovernment, and self-government will mean an ever increasing portion of a band's budget being controlled and administered by the band itself.
As we proceed with the devolution of authority and power from the Department to the bands, moving more and more to self-government, the transferring of the dollars from the Department to the band will become a smoother process.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, constitutional reform would be a good place to start, but first let me thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) for bringing forward this motion today. I think it is a very timely and important motion. Let me thank him also for the work that he has done for native people over the years, particularly in this Parliament, and for the work that he has done for our Party.
Recently he was instrumental in organizing a forum on aboriginal and First Nations issues which brought together native people from all across the country to focus for several days on important policy issues. For us as a Party it is important to revisit the fundamental problems that native people face, and the Member is also to be congratulated for that.
This motion today covers a number of important issues with regard to the native community in Canada. As I said, let me start with constitutional reform. We have just heard the suggestion that the door has not swung completely shut and that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is trying to open it again. However, I think we have to admit as politicians on both sides of the House that we have not been very effective in advancing the cause of constitutional reform on behalf of native people.
It seems to me that if Meech Lake is approved as is, with no change at all, then it will be more difficult in future for native people to obtain constitutional change. Surely that is where power rests in the country. Where do native people get power?
Supply
They get it from having enough money, from having enough local control over their own lives. They get it out of the Constitution of Canada and from political will. Yet if Meech Lake goes through unamended it will be more difficult, rather than less, for native people to bring about change in the future.
Reference was just made to a conference that came within "a hair's breadth". We all know what the "hair's breadth" was. We know there were certain parts of the country, certain people, certain politicians, who refused consent to a resolution which had widespread support. Yet those same people and politicians and areas are going to have more power in future, not less, to stop any kind of constitutional change like that.
It is not enough to say we are trying to get the door open again and get the consultation process going specifically if Meech Lake goes ahead with no change, because I do not see and native people do not see where there will be an effective constitutional opportunity for them to advance their cause in future. We have to recognize that and recognize it now because Meech Lake is coming up again and we will focus on that. That is one of the serious issues we have to deal with, and we have to demand some changes in order that that might come about because those changes are very important.
Where do many native people live? They live in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Some of them live in my riding. I have two Indian bands there. The Labrador Inuit Association has several thousand members and the Labrador Metis Association has about six to eight hundred members. I think I understand what they want. However, the great majority of native people live in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon. Apart from the effect on native people living there, those areas will themselves find it more difficult in future to achieve self-government. That is where they are going to get political power. That is an advancement of political power. Therefore, these issues are important to us when we come to discuss Meech Lake.
The other items listed in the motion are important. First, quality education and facilities for Indian children with genuine Indian control. That is so important. Look at language alone. If we do not take steps dealing with not only funding but curriculum to preserve the language, the culture will die. When the culture dies, the community is quite a different community; it is not the same at all. French Canadians have gone through that battle for many years. It is a battle over language. Why is language so important? It is because bound up in language is the essence of culture. The same thing is true of native people. If we do not put in place the proper funds and proper curriculum for native schools, if we do not emphasize native language and native culture, that will be a weakness in the process of self-determination and advancing their cause.
In my own province it is a little more difficult because we do not have any status Indians. In 1949, when we joined this country, it was agreed that funds for native people would be transferred to the province on a per capita basis. The same amount would be transferred as would normally be given to

May 11, 1988
Supply
native people in other parts of the country on a per capita basis. That is what happened and a block of funds is transferred to the province. Native people in my province want some control over how that money is spent, but they do not have that either. They do not have easy access to those funds. Decisions are still made by the two levels of government without enough control by native people in the province. It is more difficult for them to get a handle on money for education.
The whole question of education is very important. Why? It is because in any country, not just this country, it is well known that the kind of job one has, and therefore the kind of salary one makes, is directly related to one's amount of education. There is a direct correlation between the two. That is the reason we have to emphasize education for native people. I am talking about secondary education, but let me go on to another important point.
I think one of the most tragic things the Government has done is to cap the amount of money available for postsecondary education. That is exactly what has been done. I want to read a letter from the Labrador Inuit Association which says:
I understand through various media reports that you were very concerned that at the radar construction sites at Saglek, Labrador, only one position out of a possible 150 jobs was filled by a local resident.
Enclosed please find a copy of a letter from the regional Department of Indian and Northern Affairs. This letter is informing the Labrador Inuit that funds are no longer available for any vocational training programs in Labrador. Without financial assistance for occupational training the employment situation in Northern Labrador cannot be expected to improve.
Let me put that in context. I remember going to the Northwest Territories with the Standing Committee on National Defence where we heard representations concerning the North Warning System. That system was a good idea, and it needs to be done. Native people have no problems with putting it in place. They say: If you are going to come up from the south and do that, fine, but are we part of it? What are we going to get out of it? What is it in for us"?
It is in that context that I want to read that letter. It says only one position out of a possible 150 jobs was filled by local residents. Do you know why, Mr. Speaker? It is because local residents do not have a lot of training. That gets us back to the issue that I raised concerning the amount of money available for post-secondary education for native people. That amount has been capped. The Government is building the North Warning System and putting 150 jobs in the community, but it is saying to local and native people, "that is fine, but we are capping the amount of money available to you for postsecondary education. We know it is the only way you are going to get those jobs, but we are capping those funds".
I know that in government the right hand does not know what the left hand is doing. I know there is no central planning agency. Yet all the native people are asking for is reasonable opportunity. I do not think that is too much to ask for. I do not think it is too much to ask that they be able to get training so
that they can get jobs in this, one of the greatest countries in the worlds with unlimited resources. In 1988 that is not too much to ask. I really believe that if the Government has any sympathy at all, any compassion, any understanding of what needs to be done, it will reinstitute the program of postsecondary education with full funding.
Eliminating the obstacles to settlements in current claims policies, including treaty land entitlements, is another case in point. Let me start from the North Warning System again. In my area not only is the North Warning System going in, but we have low level flying in the same areas that people are hunting and fishing. I think these things can be carried on together with some safeguards, but all these activities should happen within the context of land claims.
The important thing is that native people want to deal with the North Warning System, low level flying, and industrial development in the context of land claims. The important thing for them is land claims because, unless they have some way of controlling their own lives and their own futures, they cannot deal with these issues.
Yet there is a continuous hold up of land claims. I do not think the land claims are unreasonable. I have not heard any native group say that they want complete, absolute, and utter control over what goes on in this area. They are not saying that. The Labrador Inuit Association is saying that it wants some say in the over-all future of a certain area and municipal control where people live which has to be fairly absolute. They want some input into policy at the provincial and federal levels, and they want some compensation. They want some natural resource rights.
That is not unreasonable. It is not separating a block of territory from Canada. We are not talking about an absolute Government but a reasonable approach to a reasonable degree of self-government. Unless that happens we cannot deal with the changes that are going on.
I have another letter from the Labrador Inuit Association telling me that the Memorandum of Understanding that had been agreed to by the Province of Newfoundland and the Government of Canada has now been washed down the drain. The Cabinet of Canada has rejected the Memorandum of Understanding which has been signed for a year. The Government of Newfoundland signed it a year ago, the federal Cabinet has just thrown it out, and we have to start again from square one to negotiate land claims in Labrador. The Labrador Inuit are completely frustrated and do not know where to turn.
That is a fundamental issue. Unless we are prepared to exercise the political will that is necessary to start those claims-not to settle them, just to start them, which will be a fairly long process-we are not giving the native people the power they need to determine their own future. Therefore I completely agree with the clause of the motion with regard to
May 11, 1988

eliminating the obstacles to settlement in current claims policies, including treaty land entitlements.
I dealt at the beginning of my speech with reinstating constitutional funding to aboriginal organizations and making a constitutional amendment on self-government a priority. It is essential that we do that.
I see that you are indicating that my time is running out, Mr. Speaker. As I said in the beginning, I am pleased that we had the opportunity to debate this today. I congratulate my colleague from Cochrane-Superior. I hope that the Government will see the wisdom of reinstituting these programs now in the context of the forthcoming debate on Meech Lake.

However, I could give the undertaking that we will not call quorum and, on behalf of those of us who would like to participate, perhaps the House would see fit to accept the motion of the Hon. Member. Indeed, I would second that motion if possible.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLICIES AND PROGRAMS FOR ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the point raised by the Hon. Member in terms of the importance of Baltic night. However, the issue which we are discussing today in the House of Commons applies directly to hundreds of thousands of Canadians of native origin. If we agree not to call for a quorum count, only three or four members of the government Party would be required to stay in the House of Commons to speak in the debate. That would allow 207 Members to attend the Baltic night on behalf of the Government.
I am simply seeking unanimous consent to allow this important debate to continue for another few hours.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, parliamentarians are very busy. This is also a very important evening for the young people of Canada. Many of us have to attend Adventures in Citizenship tonight. Young people from many of our ridings have come a long distance to meet with their Members of Parliament, and I am looking forward to meeting the young people of my constituency.
